```{r}
remove(list=ls())
```

About 66 million years ago, an asteroid struck the Yucatan peninsula, ending
the Cretaceous period and wiping out the non-avian dinosaurs. Placental
mammals, the group that includes primates, rodents, bats, whales, carnivores,
and most other living mammals, diversified dramatically in the aftermath. But
did the major placental lineages (the orders, such as Primates or Carnivora)
originate *before* the extinction event and simply survive it, or did they
arise *after* it, in the ecological space left behind by the dinosaurs?

Researchers have proposed three broad models:

1. **Explosive model**: both the splits *between* orders and the
   diversification *within* orders (i.e. the crown group of each order)
   happened after the K-Pg boundary
2. **Long fuse model**: the splits between orders happened before the K-Pg
   boundary, but the crown groups of most orders diversified after it
3. **Short fuse model**: both the splits between orders and the
   diversification within orders began before the K-Pg boundary

The fossil record alone has struggled to settle this, because the earliest
fossils of a group almost always postdate its true origin. In this lab, we
will use divergence time estimation to tackle the question ourselves.

## Testing the molecular clock

In lecture, we discussed using a likelihood ratio test to decide whether a
strict molecular clock is a good fit to the data. We'll do that here, keeping
the tree topology fixed to the ML tree so that the only difference between
the two models is the clock constraint.

Both models can be fit with functions from `phangorn`, starting from the
same initial tree. The clock model needs a starting tree that is rooted and
ultrametric, so we'll make one from the ML tree using the `phangorn`
function `nnls.tree()`, which takes a matrix of pairwise distances between
tips (`ape::cophenetic()` calculates this from a tree) and a tree topology:
`nnls.tree(cophenetic(tree), tree, method = "ultrametric", rooted = TRUE)`.
This keeps the topology of your rooted ML tree, but adjusts the branch
lengths so that the tree is ultrametric. Create this starting tree and plot
it:

```{r}
```
Note that the plot of the ultrametric tree will appear to have many polytomies.
This is an artifact of the non-negative least squares method that `phangorn`
uses to calculate branch lengths. The branches are in fact resolved and are just
assigned branch lengths of zero. We will fix this in a moment. 

The function `pml()` takes a tree, an alignment, and a substitution model,
and calculates the likelihood of the alignment given the tree and model. The
function `optim.pml()` takes the output of `pml()` and optimizes the branch
lengths and model parameters to maximize the likelihood. The general
workflow looks like this:

```
fit <- pml(tree, alignment, model = "GTR", k = 4)
fit <- optim.pml(fit, optNni = FALSE, optQ = TRUE, optBf = TRUE, optGamma = TRUE)
fit$logLik
```

Here, `k = 4` specifies four gamma rate categories (modelling site heterogeneity
in evolutionary rates), `optNni = FALSE` keeps the topology fixed, and `optQ`, 
`optBf`, and `optGamma` tell `optim.pml()` to optimize the substitution rates, 
base frequencies, and gamma shape parameter.

Use this workflow with your ultrametric starting tree to fit both models.
For the no clock model, use the workflow exactly as written above; because
every branch length is optimized freely, the tree will no longer be
ultrametric after optimization. (`pml()` will warn you that it unrooted the
tree; this is expected, since the no clock model is unrooted.) For the clock
model, add `optRooted = TRUE` to `optim.pml()`. This is the argument that
imposes the molecular clock: instead of optimizing each branch length
independently, it optimizes the ages of the nodes, so the tree stays rooted
and ultrametric. For more details on any of these functions, see their help
pages (e.g. `?optim.pml`). Report the log-likelihoods of both models:

```{r}
```

Using the log-likelihoods, calculate the likelihood ratio test statistic and
its p-value by hand (see lecture 7) using `pchisq()`. A few notes for implementing
this: 

- Make sure you use the correct number of degrees of freedom for this dataset. 
- Because your likelihoods are already logged, the formula becomes a subtraction 
of the log-likelihoods rather than a division of the original likelihoods.
- In `pchisq()`, make sure to set lower.tail = FALSE, because you are testing
against the upper tail of the distribution (i.e. the probability of observing
a LRT value at least as large under the null hypothesis).

```{r}
```

## Clock models and relative chronograms

The `ape` function `chronos()` converts a phylogram into a chronogram using
a method called *penalized likelihood*, which estimates the age of each node
under a choice of clock models. Without any calibration information,
`chronos()` returns a relative chronogram with the root age set to 1.

Use `chronos()` to estimate three relative chronograms from your rooted
phylogram: one under a strict clock (`model = "clock"`), one under a correlated 
relaxed clock (`model = "correlated"`), and one under an uncorrelated relaxed 
clock (`model = "relaxed"`). `chronos()` may give you warnings about convergence;
you can ignore these for this assignment. Plot your original phylogram
alongside the strict clock chronogram:

```{r}
```

What changed between the phylogram and the chronogram, and what stayed the
same? What are the units of the chronogram?

```
```

`chronos()` reports a model fit criterion called the PHIIC (penalized
likelihood information criterion) for each model, which you can access with
`attr(chronogram, "PHIIC")`. Like AIC, lower values indicate a better
balance between fit and model complexity. Report the PHIIC for each of your
three models:

```{r}
```

## Fossil calibrations

To convert a relative chronogram into an absolute chronogram, we need
information about the ages of some nodes from the fossil record. The chunk
below creates a data frame of four fossil calibrations, adapted from a
published compilation of fossil calibrations for mammals. Each calibrated
node is defined as the common ancestor of two taxa (`taxon1` and `taxon2`),
and all ages are in millions of years (Ma). Run the chunk to load the
calibrations:

```{r}
calibrations <- data.frame(
  clade   = c("Theria", "Whippomorpha", "Perissodactyla", "Catarrhini"),
  description = c("marsupials + placentals", "hippos + whales",
                  "horses + rhinos", "Old World monkeys + apes"),
  taxon1  = c("Wallaroo", "Hippo", "Horse", "Baboon"),
  taxon2  = c("Human", "FinWhale", "IndianRhin", "Human"),
  fossil  = c("Juramaia sinensis, the oldest known eutherian",
              "Pakicetus and other early stem cetaceans",
              "Earliest crown perissodactyls",
              "Earliest crown catarrhines"),
  min_age = c(156.3, 52.4, 55.0, 24.44),
  max_age = c(169.6, NA, NA, NA)
)
calibrations
```

Sources for the fossil calibrations: the minimum and maximum ages for
Theria, Whippomorpha, and Catarrhini are adapted from Table 2 of Tarver et
al. (2016), which draws on the calibrations compiled by Benton et al.
(2015). The minimum age for Perissodactyla is an approximate value based on
the earliest Eocene perissodactyl fossils, and is not taken from these
compilations.

* Benton, M. J., et al. (2015). Constraints on the timescale of animal
  evolutionary history. *Palaeontologia Electronica*, 18.1.1FC.
  https://palaeo-electronica.org/content/fc-1
* Tarver, J. E., et al. (2016). The interrelationships of placental mammals
  and the limits of phylogenetic inference. *Genome Biology and Evolution*,
  8(2), 330-344. https://academic.oup.com/gbe/article/8/2/330/2574016

`chronos()` takes calibrations as a data frame with one row per calibrated
node and the columns `node`, `age.min`, `age.max`, and `soft.bounds`. Below,
I've provided a function which will construct a dataframe for `chronos()` in
the correct format using the provided calibrations: 

```{r}
make_chronos_calib <- function(tree, calibrations, type = c("minimum", "exact"),
                               default_max = max(calibrations$max_age, na.rm = TRUE)) {
  type <- match.arg(type)
  # node number for each calibration = MRCA of its two defining taxa
  nodes <- mapply(function(a, b) ape::getMRCA(tree, c(a, b)),
                  calibrations$taxon1, calibrations$taxon2)
  age_min <- calibrations$min_age
  if (type == "exact") {
    # fossil age treated as the exact age of the node
    age_max <- calibrations$min_age
  } else {
    # fossil age treated as a minimum; missing maxima get default_max
    age_max <- ifelse(is.na(calibrations$max_age), default_max, calibrations$max_age)
  }
  data.frame(node = unname(nodes), age.min = age_min, age.max = age_max,
             soft.bounds = FALSE)
}
```

## Bayesian divergence time estimation

`chronos()` gives us a point estimate of each node age, but no measure of
uncertainty. To get one, we will do Bayesian divergence time estimation with
`MrBayes`, which you installed in Lab 6. Because a full analysis that also
estimates the topology would take hours on a laptop, we will fix the topology
to the maximum-likelihood tree and only estimate node ages. The function
below writes a MrBayes input file containing the alignment, your tree, and a
`MRBAYES` block with the analysis settings. Run the chunk to define the
function:

```{r}
write_mrbayes_dating <- function(tree, alignment, file, calibrations,
                                 tree_age, ngen = 500000) {
  # alignment and tree tips must match
  stopifnot(setequal(tree$tip.label, names(alignment)))
  tree$edge.length <- NULL
  tree$node.label <- NULL
  phangorn::write.phyDat(alignment, file, format = "nexus")
  cat("\nBEGIN TREES;\n  TREE mltree = ", ape::write.tree(tree),
      "\nEND;\n", file = file, append = TRUE, sep = "")

  constraint_lines <- sapply(names(calibrations), function(cl)
    paste0("  constraint ", cl, " = ",
           paste(calibrations[[cl]]$taxa, collapse = " "), ";"))
  calibrate_lines <- sapply(names(calibrations), function(cl)
    paste0("  calibrate ", cl, " = ", calibrations[[cl]]$prior, ";"))

  block <- c(
    "",
    "BEGIN MRBAYES;",
    "  set autoclose=yes;",
    "  lset nst=6 rates=gamma;",
    constraint_lines,
    calibrate_lines,
    "  prset brlenspr = clock:uniform;",
    paste0("  prset topologypr = constraints(",
           paste(names(calibrations), collapse = ", "), ");"),
    paste0("  prset treeagepr = ", tree_age, ";"),
    "  prset nodeagepr = calibrated;",
    "  prset clockvarpr = igr;",
    "  prset clockratepr = lognormal(-6, 1);",
    paste0("  mcmcp ngen=", format(ngen, scientific = FALSE),
           " samplefreq=500 printfreq=10000 diagnfreq=10000",
           " nchains=1 nruns=2;"),
    "  startvals tau = mltree;",
    "  propset ExtSprClock(Tau,V)$prob=0 NNIClock(Tau,V)$prob=0 ParsSPRClock(Tau,V)$prob=0;",
    "  mcmc;",
    "  sump;",
    "  sumt;",
    "END;"
  )
  cat(block, file = file, append = TRUE, sep = "\n")
  invisible(file)
}
```

The `calibrations` argument is a named list with one entry per calibrated
node, each containing all of the taxa that belong to the node and a MrBayes
prior on its age. The `tree_age` argument is the prior on the age of the
root (here, the split between the platypus and all other mammals). Here are
the calibrations from the `calibrations` data frame, treating each fossil
age as a minimum bound:

```{r}
calib <- list(
  theria         = list(taxa  = setdiff(names(Laurasiatherian), "Platypus"),
                        prior = "uniform(156.3, 169.6)"),
  whippomorpha   = list(taxa  = c("Hippo", "FinWhale", "BlueWhale",
                                  "SpermWhale"),
                        prior = "offsetexponential(52.4, 57.4)"),
  perissodactyla = list(taxa  = c("Horse", "Donkey", "WhiteRhino",
                                  "IndianRhin"),
                        prior = "offsetexponential(55.0, 60.0)"),
  catarrhini     = list(taxa  = c("Baboon", "Human"),
                        prior = "offsetexponential(24.44, 29.44)")
)
```

Run the analysis at the command line with `mb lab9_mammals.nex`. This may take
a while, depending on your machine. When it finishes, the file ending in `.con.tre`
contains the consensus tree with summaries of the posterior distribution of
each node age. As in Lab 6, this file is in an unusual format, so the helper
function below will load it for you. It returns a list containing the tree
(with median node ages as node labels) and a data frame with the median and
95% highest posterior density (HPD) interval of the age of each node:

```{r}
read_mrbayes_ages <- function(file) {
  txt <- paste(readLines(file, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n")

  # translate table: tip numbers -> taxon names
  block <- regmatches(txt, regexpr("(?si)translate.*?;", txt, perl = TRUE))
  block <- sub(";\\s*$", "", sub("^\\s*translate", "", block))
  entries <- trimws(strsplit(block, ",")[[1]])
  entries <- entries[nzchar(entries)]
  tr_map <- setNames(sub("^\\S+\\s+", "", entries), sub("\\s.*$", "", entries))

  # consensus tree statement
  nwk <- regmatches(txt, regexpr(
    "(?i)tree\\s+con_50_majrule\\s*=\\s*(\\[&[RU]\\]\\s*)?[^;]*;", txt,
    perl = TRUE))
  nwk <- sub("^[^=]*=\\s*(\\[&[RU]\\]\\s*)?", "", nwk)

  # replace internal node annotations with temporary labels
  ann <- regmatches(nwk, gregexpr("\\[&[^]]*\\]", nwk))[[1]]
  pieces <- strsplit(nwk, "\\[&[^]]*\\]")[[1]]
  out <- pieces[1]
  node_ann <- character(0)
  for (i in seq_along(ann)) {
    if (grepl("\\)$", out)) {
      node_ann <- c(node_ann, ann[i])
      out <- paste0(out, "N", length(node_ann))
    }
    if (i + 1 <= length(pieces)) out <- paste0(out, pieces[i + 1])
  }
  out <- gsub("\\s+", "", out)

  # tip numbers -> names
  m <- gregexpr("(?<=[(,])[0-9]+(?=[:,)])", out, perl = TRUE)
  regmatches(out, m) <- list(unname(tr_map[regmatches(out, m)[[1]]]))
  phy <- ape::read.tree(text = out)

  get_value <- function(a, key)
    as.numeric(sub(paste0(".*\\b", key, "=([0-9.eE+-]+).*"), "\\1", a))
  get_hpd <- function(a, i) {
    v <- sub(".*age_95%HPD=\\{([^}]*)\\}.*", "\\1", a)
    as.numeric(sapply(strsplit(v, ","), `[`, i))
  }

  idx <- as.integer(sub("^N", "", phy$node.label))
  ages <- data.frame(node       = ape::Ntip(phy) + seq_len(ape::Nnode(phy)),
                     age_median = get_value(node_ann[idx], "age_median"),
                     hpd_lower  = get_hpd(node_ann[idx], 1),
                     hpd_upper  = get_hpd(node_ann[idx], 2))
  phy$node.label <- round(ages$age_median, 1)
  list(tree = phy, ages = ages)
}
```

The code below will load the consensus tree (obtained from read_mrbayes_ages)
and plot it with the 95% HPDinterval of each node age shown as a bar, 
a time axis, and a vertical line at  66 Ma marking the K-Pg boundary. 
Run it to generate the plot (you may have to change the path to your version of 
the output file from MrBayes): 

```{r}
mb <- read_mrbayes_ages("lab9_mammals.nex.con.tre")
mb_tree <- mb$tree
mb_ages <- mb$ages

# Plot the tree, leaving space on the left so the oldest HPD bars aren't cut off
plot(mb_tree, cex = 0.6, label.offset = 1,
     x.lim = c(-0.15 * max(mb_ages$hpd_upper), max(mb_ages$hpd_upper) * 1.15))

# Plotting coordinates of every node
pp <- get("last_plot.phylo", envir = .PlotPhyloEnv)
n <- mb_ages$node

# 95% HPD intervals as semi-transparent bars at each node
segments(x0 = pp$xx[n] + (mb_ages$age_median - mb_ages$hpd_upper),
         x1 = pp$xx[n] + (mb_ages$age_median - mb_ages$hpd_lower),
         y0 = pp$yy[n], col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.4), lwd = 5, lend = 1)

# Time axis and the K-Pg boundary (66 Ma before the tips)
axisPhylo(backward = TRUE)
mtext("Millions of years ago", side = 1, line = 2.5, cex = 0.8)
kpg_x <- max(pp$xx[1:Ntip(mb_tree)]) - 66
abline(v = kpg_x, lty = 2, col = "red")
text(kpg_x, Ntip(mb_tree) + 1, "K-Pg", col = "red", cex = 0.7, pos = 4, xpd = TRUE)
```

Is there a relationship between the age of a node and the uncertainty of its
age estimate? Give at least one reason why we might expect this.
